title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: a challenging diagnosis established at autopsy
case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of tongue paresthesia, slurred speech, and progressive weakness. The weakness began on the left side and later involved the right side; he also noted decreased sensitivity in the left half of his body. He denied fever, headache, weight loss, dyspnea, convulsions, visual symptoms, incontinence, and vertigo. His only risk factors were a 15 pack-year smoking history and occasional alcohol use. 

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic examination showed hyposensitivity of the right hemiface and right side of the body, and grade 4/5 strength in the left upper limb. The remainder of the physical and neurologic examinations was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits. HIV testing by ELISA and Western blot was positive; the CD4+ count was 75 cells/µL, and the HIV-1 RNA viral load was 97 911 copies/mL. Noncontrast brain CT showed two hypodense foci in the right frontal and high parietal white matter without contrast enhancement or midline shift. Given the CT findings in an HIV-positive patient, pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine were started for presumed neurotoxoplasmosis.

Two weeks later, there was no clinical improvement; toxoplasma IgG and IgM serologies were negative, and follow-up CT showed enlargement of the lesions. Brain MRI demonstrated extensive, discontinuous hyperintense areas on T2- and FLAIR-weighted images involving the hemispheric white matter—predominantly in the right frontotemporal subcortical region—as well as lesions in the splenium of the corpus callosum and the brainstem.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. The initial working diagnosis was neurotoxoplasmosis because of HIV infection and CT lesions — “Due to the imaging findings in a patient with HIV, neurotoxoplasmosis was the initial working diagnosis.”  
2. Lack of response to anti-toxoplasma therapy argued against toxoplasmosis — “the patient’s clinical features did not improve;”  
3. Negative toxoplasma serology further excluded toxoplasmosis — “the serology for toxoplasmosis tested negative for immunoglobulin IgG and IgM;”  
4. Lesion progression on CT despite therapy made toxoplasmosis unlikely — “the lesions increased in size and became more evident in controlled CT;”  
5. PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in CSF was negative, ruling out CNS tuberculosis — “PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis … was negative;”  
6. PCR for Cryptococcus spp in CSF was negative, excluding cryptococcal infection — “PCR for … Cryptococcus spp … was negative;”  
7. PCR for Toxoplasma gondii in CSF was negative, further excluding reactivated toxoplasmosis — “PCR for … Toxoplasma gondii … was negative;”  
8. The MRI lesion characteristics—multifocal, nonenhancing white-matter hyperintensities without mass effect—were most consistent with PML — “extensive discontinuous hyper signal areas on T2- and FLAIR-weighted images in the hemispheric white matter, with predominance in the right frontotemporal subcortical region…”
